title: Diet Drinks or Water? A Two-Year Weight Study
paragraphs: Few staples of the modern diet attract as much ambivalence as the diet soft drink, simultaneously recommended as a means of cutting sugar and suspected of whetting the appetite and covertly frustrating weight loss. A two-year randomised trial conducted by researchers at the universities of Liverpool and Leeds, and published in the British Journal of Nutrition, suggests that the latter anxiety may be misplaced.

The SWITCH trial allocated 493 adults with overweight or obesity at random to water or to commercially available beverages sweetened with aspartame, acesulfame-K or sucralose, embedding both arms in a structured behavioural weight-management programme whose withdrawal in the final year served to test whether participants could sustain their results unaided.

Among completers, the diet-beverage arm had shed 4.8 kilograms and the water arm 3.7, a disparity that fell short of statistical significance and that the authors construe as evidence of equivalence rather than superiority. The conclusions nonetheless warrant circumspection: the study was underwritten by the American Beverage Association, notwithstanding the investigators’ assurances of analytical independence, confined to a single site and depleted by substantial attrition, and it sits awkwardly with World Health Organization guidance cautioning against reliance on non-sugar sweeteners for weight control.

questions.q: What does the word “ambivalence” in the first sentence refer to?
questions.a: The mixed view of diet drinks as both helpful for cutting sugar and suspected of harming weight loss.

questions.q: What is meant by “attrition” in the final paragraph?
questions.a: Participants dropping out of the study over time.

questions.q: Why does the article distinguish between equivalence and superiority?
questions.a: The data suggest diet drinks are about as effective as water, not that they are more effective.
